catalog_quote: [Wilde 2016 §2.3, p.135] Gamāle Khām contrasts between modal (14a) and breathy (14b) phonation. ... In Wilde (2011: 279,287) I considered whether Gamāle Khām phonology may also feature tense phonation. However, further investigation has led to the conclusion that this is not the case, and that the stiff voice or laryngealisation is an idiolectal tendency and/or caused variably by syllable-final glottal restriction. Unlike Takāle Khām as described by Watters (1971; 1985; 2002), Gamāle Khām is an atonal language. A pitch distinction was encountered with any certainty only once in the corpus (15a–b). ... [Wilde 2017 §2.1.3, p.71] Vowel length is non-contrastive. For the most part also pitch is non-contrastive. A pitch distinction was encountered with any certainty only once in the corpus (19a–b). ... audit.reasoning: The record codes Gamale Kham UNDETERMINED because none of the three dedicated phonological descriptions (Wilde 2011, 2016, 2017) states, locates or denies word stress; I re-opened all three held texts at the cited loci and confirmed every quoted sentence verbatim with correct page numbers, and full-text greps confirm 'stress' appears only in the 2011 abstract disclaimer and a Takale clitic gloss in 2017. These are the best and only phonological sources for this languoid per Glottolog and a Crossref sweep; the remaining unheld items (Moore 2019 MA morphology thesis; Wilde 2017 LTBA historical paper) are unlikely to contain a stress rule. Nothing was fetched sources beyond bibliographic records (saved with under. Coding and evidence grade stand; no action.
